en: It was his tender cradle age;
Then little Semetey
Was laughing and laughing.
Your sister-in-law suffered grief;
Then she was in a state she could not bear.
Above, God's sun grew overcast;
Sixty sorrows came upon her head at once.
Her rib bones seemed to come apart,
Her tears flowed;
Then her heart was terribly distracted.
Her dear hair, thick as a girth,
She wound tightly upon her crown.
A black, white-blazed thoroughbred,
The fierce woman saddled and mounted.
At his tender cradle age,
She held Semetey before her;
The generous leopard Manas,
She went out to meet him.
Your wondrous sister-in-law
Surpassed herself in marvels:
“The sultan will come home ill,” she thought.
“The dear handful of people
Will lose heart,” she thought.
Her black, white-blazed thoroughbred,
She turned toward the high bank.
The cradle-age child beneath her arm,
She pinched sharply, twisting his flesh;
She struck the child, making him scream.
When she pinched his flesh with a twist,
“Waa, waa, waa, waa,” the baby cried;
The baby cried loudly, screaming.
As the baby screamed and cried,
He cried until it pierced the ears and brain.
That mighty Manas upon the bier
Rose up, looming large.
His good fortune when sent ahead,
His sworn companion Bakai, his vast army—
“What a dreadful, bellowing sound!
Take heed, leopard Bakai.
She was a malicious slave-woman;
Kanykey seems to be burning with grief on the high bank:
‘When he hears the child's voice,
Let him take courage,’ she thought;
She must have given the child a painful pinch.
‘Ee, ee, ee, ee,’ he cries;
The baby cries loudly, screaming.
These screaming sounds
Pierce the ears and brain with crying.
He is my soft, mottled gray falcon;
To me, a gray goshawk, a morning star.
He is a spring flowing through the valley;
He is the dear child of my late years.
If I see him, my heart will be content.
My blue-maned Bakai, wait a moment;
I have no support but my child.
Almambet and Chubak, precious souls—
Bakai, whenever I remember them, I burn.
For my dear child, my tireless, swift steed,
I keep asking God to grant him life.”
Then he loomed large in fury,
His bloodthirst seized him fiercely.
Setting aside his many sorrows,
Taking the child as his support,
The sacred Bozkise belt,
He girded tightly about his waist.
Manas, the dear lion blessed by Kydyr,
Then cried aloud, “Islam!”
His bulletproof white padded armor,
As though entering battle,
He had put it on.
Arbuudan, the powerfully backed racer—
Manas girded himself over his armor;
Your champion Manas, the leopard,
Had mounted him.
Mounted, he swayed and turned,
Gathered himself like a lion.
As your generous Manas stood,
That beauty of dark complexion,
The radiant one among the Muslims,
The youngest of twelve daughters,
God's beloved servant,
Girded with a belt of gold,
Light shining upon her moon-like face,
Before your generous one,
Poor Kanykey emerged, downcast.
When she saw the champion's face,
Your unfortunate one stood solemnly;
That was where she faced the man:
“Great Beijing, from which none return—
My sovereign, have you come back safe and sound?
Fortunate when sent into battle,
All those champions,
Did you give them to Beijing as a gift?
My sovereign, even the sleek bay among horses has passed;
Not just the heroes Almambet and Chubak,
Even the ancient lion, holy Ali, has passed.
My lord, what we see today is gone tomorrow.
The deceiver keeps deceiving;
Hero, such is this mischievous world!
There is no gain in grieving for the dead.”
After Manas turned back,
After his wedded lady spoke her solemn counsel:
“My fierce one, do not distract my thoughts.
Bring here to me
The child of my late years.
My soft, mottled gray falcon,
Bring him here to me,
My gray goshawk, my morning star,
Whom I opened my mouth to kiss,
Whom I opened my eyes to see.”
Though he spoke, the unfortunate woman would not agree;
She would not give her child to the lion hero.
The swaddled child,
She held close, hiding him.
The reason she hid him:
Your hero was the support of the faith,
His fortune was complete;
Your hero was a lion upheld by holy patrons.
If you looked within him,
He was broader than the face of the earth.
Whoever he looked at did not survive.
Her sovereign, Khan Manas,
Was not one to caress a child.
The reason he did not caress children:
Whoever he looked at did not survive.
There was a black mark in his eye,
There was dreadful venom in his face.
Kanykey knew his secret;
Crying out, she would not give him to the champion.
Kanykey, who had seen and knew,
Sobbing, would not give him to the blue-maned one.
When his recourse had utterly failed,
Zulpukor, held by Khan Manas,
To the child he had so greatly missed,
The hero gave his whip as a gift.
As your hero held out his whip,
She grasped the whip, making the token known,
Touched it to Semetey's forehead.
The whip that had touched his forehead,
He could only kiss, kiss, kiss;
The unfortunate khan drew strength from it,
Kissing it, saying, “God has given him to me.”
When they drew nearer,
The edge of Talas came into view.
“Almambet, Chubak, my precious ones!”
The leopard's heart was terribly torn.
Your hero, known as hero Manas,
His dear eyes like a saker's,
Without blinking, tears in his eyes,
Who had gathered an army to strike the governors,
His heart burned fiercely with grief.
Your hero broke into tears, crying aloud.
His golden-cheeked battle-axe,
He grasped at its throat and turned;
The hero braced it against his side.
Your hero raised his voice in a wail.
At Almambet's and Chubak's royal tents,
Your hero fell to loud lamentation:
“I let Akkula fall to a bullet, dear friend.
Golden forelock, tasseled belt, dear friend,
Azizkan's only son, dear friend,
I sent Almambet to martyrdom, dear friend.
My wings were broken, dear friend;
Seated in mourning,
I have lost Khan Chubak, dear friend!
I raided Beijing and took much, dear friend.
Consider all souls: none could match him;
I have devoured my Syrgak, dear friend.
I let bullets tear away my wings, dear friend.
Parted from my leopard,
I stilled my life in a dreadful day, dear friend!
From Beijing beyond Solomon's reach, dear friend,
I wrested its dominion, dear friend.
Seeking to claim its dominion, dear friend,
I have devoured my twins, dear friend!
I entered Beijing and returned, dear friend;
I was parted from my champions, dear friend.
I let my wings be caught by fire, dear friend.
All my leopards,
I lost to the imperial Chinese, dear friend!
My pair of twin lambs, dear friend,
Having devoured both together,
How can I go on without dying, dear friend!
Black Beijing, the imperial Chinese, dear friend,
Did I not keep them besieged, dear friend?
I subdued the Shibee and the lamas, dear friend;
I did not die while beating them, dear friend.
Were all there, I did not die, dear friend!
While the lions Almambet, Chubak and Syrgak
Were all there, I did not die, dear friend!
I let Beijing bring me distress, dear friend.
Coveting great wealth,
I was parted from my champions, dear friend!”
When Khan Manas arrived thus,
The birches wept, the willows wept;
Then all the multitude of people wept.
The rosy young girls,
In place of red, they dressed in mourning;
The fully mature women,
In place of black, they dressed in mourning.
Among horses, the pied-headed steed—
Heroes, Argyn and Kyrgyz together,
The old men of ninety wept,
All the assembled people wept,
Those drunk on liquor wept,
The heedless and thoughtless,
Then the twelve-year-old youngsters wept.
The full-grown warriors wept;
Khan Manas's forty fierce champions all wept.
Then Aruuke, Agynai's daughter,
Almambet's wife:
“The horses in the mountains are nine vast herds,
Thoroughbreds and swift steeds together.
A bad name awaits me;
Do not leave my soul desolate and scorched.
My mountain, my lord, take me with you!
My sovereign, we joined when thumb-sized,
Or united when tiny as lice.
Bind me to your saddle-thong;
To go beside you as a companion,
Leopard, take wretched me with you!
My dresses of many kinds,
When I pull them up, will not reach my neck.
Do not exhaust this unfortunate one;
Leopard, draw me into your embrace!
If thirty rivers joined,
My sovereign was like their rushing stretch;
If thirty mountains joined,
My sovereign was like their narrow pass.”
Crying aloud in lament,
Then Almambet's wife Aruuke,
Chubak's wife Byrmyskal,
Burulcha, Esenkan's daughter,
Then before Khan Manas,
Grieving, weeping, crying aloud,
Before your sovereign,
Oh hero, three ladies came sobbing.
All three had bloody, torn faces,
Their black hair hanging loose.
From their radiant, moon-like cheeks,
Then blood flowed in channels and channels.
From their dear, currant-like eyes,
Tears flowed a whip's length.
From their dear eyes like a quail's,
Tears flowed in separate streams.
When one looked, their faces were torn;
Bloody tears, mingled with blood,
Poured the length of a ditch:
“Dear friend, when the moon grows dark,
What shall we do with the night?
Our precious ones left no son behind;
What shall we do with the day?
Nine thousand horses in the mountains,
There is no master to hold them in check.
What God has brought upon us,
Oh hero, we have no choice but to bear.
